content: In geometry, two lines or planes (or a line and a plane) are considered perpendicular, or orthogonal, if they form congruent adjacent angles. The term perpendicular can be used as either a noun or an adjective. For example, in Figure 1, the line AB is perpendicular to the line CD at the point B. By definition, a line is infinitely long, so AB and CD in this context represent line segments of two infinitely long lines. Even if the line segments AB and CD do not physically intersect, they are still considered perpendicular if their extensions to infinity form congruent adjacent angles. Conversely, any lines that meet to form right angles are defined as perpendicular. In a coordinate plane, perpendicular lines have slopes that are opposite reciprocals of each other. For example, a horizontal line has a slope of zero, while a vertical line has an undefined slope (sometimes described as ±infinity). Two lines are perpendicular if their slopes multiply to -1. This relationship is denoted mathematically as perpendicular. Slopes in Cartesian Coordinates In a Cartesian coordinate system, two straight lines, L and M, can be described by their equations, provided neither line is vertical. If the slopes of these lines are denoted as a and c, then the lines are perpendicular if and only if the product of their slopes equals -1 (i.e., ac = -1). Vertical lines are always perpendicular to horizontal lines, and vice versa. For example, any horizontal line described by y = K (where K is a constant) is perpendicular to any vertical line described by x = J (where J is a constant). Constructing a Perpendicular Line To construct a line perpendicular to a given line AB through a specific point P using a compass and straightedge, follow these steps: 1. Draw a circle centered at P that intersects the line AB at two points, A' and B', which are equidistant from P. 2. Draw two additional circles, one centered at A' and the other at B', both passing through P. Let Q be the second point of intersection of these two circles. 3. Connect P and Q to form the desired perpendicular line PQ. To prove that PQ is perpendicular to AB, use the Side-Side-Side (SSS) congruence theorem for triangles QPA' and QPB' to show that the angles OPA' and OPB' are equal. Then, apply the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) congruence theorem to triangles OPA' and OPB' to conclude that the angles POA and POB are equal, confirming that PQ is perpendicular to AB. Perpendicularity and Parallel Lines If two lines (a and b) are both perpendicular to a third line (c), then all the angles formed at the intersections with the third line are right angles. In Euclidean geometry, this means that lines a and b are parallel to each other, as stated by the parallel postulate. Conversely, if one line is perpendicular to a second line, it is also perpendicular to any line parallel to the second line. In Figure 3, all orange-shaded angles are congruent to each other, and all green-shaded angles are congruent to each other. This is because vertical angles are congruent, and alternate interior angles formed by a transversal cutting parallel lines are also congruent. Therefore, if lines a and b are parallel, the following conclusions are equivalent: One of the angles in the diagram is a right angle. One of the orange-shaded angles is congruent to one of the green-shaded angles. Line c is perpendicular to line a. Line c is perpendicular to line b. Finding Perpendicular Lines in Algebra For any linear equation of the form y = mx + b, the slope of a perpendicular line will be the opposite reciprocal of the original slope, or -1/m. A helpful mnemonic is flip the fraction and change the sign to find the slope of a perpendicular line. For example, if the slope of the original line is a whole number a, it can be written as a/1, and the perpendicular slope would be -1/a. To find the equation of a perpendicular line that passes through a specific point (x, y), substitute the known values of m, x, and y into the equation y = (-1/m)x + b, and solve for b. Finding Perpendicular Lines in Calculus In calculus, the slope of a curve at a specific point (x, y) is determined by finding the derivative of the function. This derivative represents the slope (m) of the tangent line at that point. To find the equation of a perpendicular line, use the slope -1/m (the opposite reciprocal of the derivative) and substitute the known values of m, x, and y into the equation y = (-1/m)x + b to solve for b.
